name: Omar Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Mr Hollins at Scar Top, which is a hill farm, about eleven hundred ewes on open hill and rough grazing, with a few fields of hay in the valley bottom. My day depends on the season. Now it's tupping, when the rams go in with the ewes, so I'm checking the rams, moving groups, and feeding on the low ground. In spring it's lambing, and you basically live in the lambing shed for six weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being up on the top on a clear morning with the dog, Nell, working sheep across the hill, and you can see three valleys. What wears me out is the weather, the rain sideways for days, and that I'm still a poor shepherd next to Mr Hollins. He can count a running flock in his head. I'm still counting twice and getting different answers.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, once I've seen they work. I'll ask one what might be wrong with a lamb before I ring the vet, and I use one to check the forms for moving sheep. I'm not chasing it, but I'm not afraid of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, like a good stick or a good dog, but not a replacement for either. I'd say that at the mart and at the mosque after Friday prayers if anyone asked. I'm not big online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it changes nothing for me. Sheep on a hill are sheep on a hill. It might make the paperwork lighter, which would be nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Mr Hollins and build up my own flock. I've got forty ewes of my own on rented grazing two miles down the valley, and I'd try to get to sixty by next autumn. I'd keep my savings steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A good, ordinary year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your own forty ewes.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought them two years ago with money I'd saved working on building sites in my early twenties. My father helped with the first rent on the grazing. Between them and the savings, I've got well over a year covered if anything happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think of you farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father had a shop in town, and he wanted me to take it on. He was disappointed at first. Now he comes up at lambing and holds the torch and tells everyone at the mosque about his son the shepherd.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool, like a good stick or a good dog, but no replacement for either. I'd say that at the cattle market or after Friday prayers if asked.
S0.think: I think it changes nothing for me, because sheep on a hill are sheep on a hill. It might just make the paperwork lighter.
S0.do: Keeps working for Mr Hollins and aims to grow his own flock from forty to sixty ewes by next autumn. Keeps his savings steady.
S0.quote: Now he comes up at lambing and holds the torch and tells everyone at the mosque about his son the shepherd.
S0.fieldNote: Omar's cushion is partly forty ewes of his own, bought with building-site savings and help from his father. Family and faith are central and come up early. He's modest about his shepherding and uses AI only once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say young people need a way in, and the best way is apprenticeships on farms, with a fair wage. Not schemes where they sit in a classroom. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't scare me for myself. I'm in, and I've got my own flock. But hill farms are already short of young people, and if they hire fewer beginners, there'll be nobody left on the hills in twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Hollins if he'd take on a lad or lass from the village for lambing, and I'd offer to train them. I'd keep building my own flock. And I'd maybe try one of those apps that count sheep from a drone, if the farm next door has had good luck with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the hills more than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the farm next door tried the drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the Bells. They say it's good for finding ewes stuck in the bracken, which saves hours. It's no good in fog, though, and we get a lot of fog. So I'd wait and see one more winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farms, mostly, with a bit of help to start. And families, too, by pushing their kids to work. My father made me work in the shop from twelve, and I'm grateful now, though I wasn't then.

S1.say: I'd say young people need a way in through farm apprenticeships with a fair wage, not classroom schemes. I'd say that to anyone.
S1.think: It doesn't scare me for myself, because I'm in and have my own flock. But hill farms are already short of young people, and with fewer beginners there'll be nobody on the hills in twenty years.
S1.do: Asks Mr Hollins to take on a village youngster for lambing and offers to train them. Keeps growing his flock and waits one more winter to see how a neighbour's sheep-counting drone copes with fog.
S1.feel: Uneasy about the future of the hills more than about himself.
S1.quote: If they hire fewer beginners, there'll be nobody left on the hills in twenty years.
S1.fieldNote: His concern is for the future of hill farming as a whole. The drone story shows his steady style: watch the neighbours, wait for proof, mind the fog. He credits his father's strictness about work, which fits his views on family and apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard on office workers, but people have to adapt, and families have to help each other. I wouldn't want the government paying people to sit at home. I'd say help them retrain, sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry for my wife, Ayesha. She works on reception at the doctors' surgery, and a lot of that is booking and forms. For me, nothing much changes on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ayesha not to panic, we've got the savings and the sheep. If her hours got cut, I'd ask her to help with my flock and the paperwork for a bit, while she looks at what's next. I might try one of those new AI tools for the sheep records, once Mr Hollins has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, worried for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ayesha feel about helping with the sheep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd laugh, she hates the smell. But she's brilliant with numbers and she'd have my flock records sorted in a week. She already tells me I'm useless with paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is to blame, if her job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like blaming. The surgery has to save money, and the tool is cheaper. If anything, the people who should help are the ones who make money from it, through their own businesses, not through taxes.

S2.say: I'd say it's hard on office workers, but people have to adapt and families should help each other. Help them retrain, but don't pay people to sit at home.
S2.think: I'd worry for my wife Ayesha, who works on reception at the doctors' surgery doing booking and forms. For me, nothing much changes on the hill.
S2.do: Reassures Ayesha that their savings and sheep give them time. Asks her to help with his flock records if her hours are cut, and tries an AI tool for sheep records once Mr Hollins has.
S2.feel: Calm for himself, worried for his wife.
S2.quote: She'd laugh, she hates the smell. But she's brilliant with numbers and she'd have my flock records sorted in a week.
S2.fieldNote: His free-market views show in wanting the firms that gain to help through their own businesses rather than through taxes. His plan for Ayesha is warm and practical. He avoids blaming anyone, which is a consistent trait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there needs to be fairness, but it shouldn't be the government taking everyone's money. Business people and families need to step up. I'd say the mosque and the churches will be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be safe. The hill's physical work, and my forty ewes would still need a shepherd. But Ayesha would probably lose her job, and I'd be watching people I know at the mosque struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep Ayesha home with me if she wanted, and maybe expand my flock, since we'd have time and the hills are safe. I'd help through the mosque, maybe giving lamb to families who are struggling at Eid. I wouldn't buy anything at boom prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe, but heavy-hearted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Giving lamb at Eid, is that something you do already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a few, through the mosque. In this picture I'd give more. My father always said the sheep are a blessing, and blessings are meant to be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more land, if the hills are safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, but not at boom prices, no. I'd rather rent more grazing and wait. Land prices go mad when people are scared and rich at the same time.

S3.say: I'd say there needs to be fairness, but not the government taking everyone's money. Business people and families need to step up, and the mosques and churches will be busy.
S3.think: Privately I'd be safe, since hill work is physical and my ewes still need a shepherd. But Ayesha would likely lose her job and I'd see people at the mosque struggling.
S3.do: Keeps Ayesha at home with him if she wants and grows his flock while the hills are safe. Gives more lamb to struggling families through the mosque at Eid and rents grazing rather than buying land at boom prices.
S3.quote: Land prices go mad when people are scared and rich at the same time.
S3.fieldNote: Omar sees this picture as a time to share, using faith and family rather than the state. He's careful not to buy at the top. The lamb at Eid is a concrete, personal way of helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on the hill would be a mistake, but I'd also say farmers have the right to buy what they want. If they work, they work. I'd tell people to wait and see if they can handle the weather first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think they'd work up there, not yet. A robot that can walk up the top in sideways rain hasn't been built. When it is, I'll want to buy one, not work for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch closely, and see what the Bells and other farms buy. I'd move more of my time onto my own flock, because owning sheep is safer than being paid to look after someone else's. If the robots work, I'd buy one with my savings, maybe with two other small farmers, to share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frightened. Ready, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your job at Scar Top?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Mr Hollins buys robots, he'll need fewer men, and I'm the junior. I'd be sad, but I'd have my own flock and maybe a robot by then. I'd still help him at lambing for nothing if he asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots on the hill would be a mistake, but also that you'd buy one. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, a bit. I think it'd be a mistake for the hills, for the young people and the way of life. But if it happens anyway, I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.

S4.say: I'd say robots on the hill would be a mistake, but farmers have the right to buy what they want. I'd tell people to wait and see if they cope with the weather first.
S4.think: I don't think robots would work up on the hill yet, in sideways rain. When they do, I'd want to buy one, not work for one.
S4.do: Watches what neighbouring farms buy and shifts more time onto his own flock. If the robots prove themselves, buys one from his savings, perhaps shared with two other small farmers.
S4.feel: Anxious but not frightened, and ready.
S4.quote: A robot that can walk up the top in sideways rain hasn't been built. When it is, I'll want to buy one, not work for one.
S4.fieldNote: Omar holds a real tension: robots are bad for the hills, but he'd rather own one than be replaced by one. His savings and his own flock let him think like an owner. He'd still help Mr Hollins at lambing for nothing, which says a lot about him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robot one. Not because I'm scared for me, I've got my sheep, but because it'd empty the hills of people. What would help is help for young people to own a few sheep and rent grazing, and a way for small farmers to share a robot instead of the big farms buying everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the dogs. Nobody asks about the dogs. A good sheepdog takes three years to train, and if robots take over, all that knowledge goes too.

headlineQuote: I'd rather own the robot than be replaced by it.
portrait: Omar is a 27-year-old junior shepherd on a hill sheep farm who owns forty ewes of his own, bought with building-site savings and his father's help. He uses AI now and then once it's proven, waits to see how neighbours' drones cope with fog, and is modest about his shepherding next to his boss. His views are traditional and free-market: families, faith and business stepping up rather than the state, and he rarely blames anyone. He worries for his wife Ayesha in the office pictures and for the hills in the slow one, and in the robot picture he thinks like an owner, planning to share a robot with other small farmers rather than work for one.
biggestWorry: The robot picture, not for himself but because it would empty the hills of people.
whatWouldHelp: Help for young people to own a few sheep and rent grazing, and a way for small farmers to share a robot instead of big farms buying everything.
